video_title: A Body Blow? The War on Iran and U.S. Military Readiness
transcript: What is military readiness actually and how has it been degraded in the US military's case due to the war against Iran and what does that mean for US and allied interests in the rest of the world and these are the questions that we start to grapple with in this episode with Mark Canian of CSIS Stacy Petty John of the Center for New American Security and Michael Eisento of the Washington Institute. Enjoy the show. How do we think about how ready the US military is? We talk about readiness a lot. We mean lots of different things by that. Brad Carson wrote an article first years ago called the chicken is ready to eat which pun on ready means lots of things. You know, going around the table, how should we think about what readiness actually means? >> Well, you have to start with the question ready for what? If you're thinking about a conflict with China, you want to bring in a variety of considerations about munitions, for example, and posture. Something that Cuba very different set of considerations. Most people think about it in terms of the ability to for a unit to execute the missions that it's designed for. And the US puts a lot of money into readiness. So on the whole, our forces are at much higher ready level of readiness than most nations keep their forces at. >> I think Mark's exactly right that it is ready for what? Dick Beth had that great book years ago, decades ago now, uh on readiness, and you need to think about whether you're considering the material, the people, and then sort of uh stockpiles of different things that they need along the way. And the big debate in up until this point had been whether you're ready to deploy. That was feeding the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan, having the new BCTs to go in and having sufficient readiness so that you could undertake operations that were needed right now versus being ready to hopefully deter, but ready in case you needed to defend against a great power adversary. and sort of conserving that readiness and focusing your training on high-end operations and making sure that you can conduct across that full spectrum versus the more narrow set that US military forces are often asked to undertake in lesser contingencies. If I could broaden the aperture a little bit here and and talk in terms of conceptual readiness or cognitive readiness in terms of our policy makers having the skills with regard to deterrence, with regard to infra deterrence, with regard to escalation management that are required in order to conduct a limited war. This is something which we've actually learned quite a bit about just in the last couple of years with regard to Iran and it seems to have gone all out the window in this current war that things that the Israelis learned in 2024 we learned in 2025 with the Israelis were forgotten very quickly and it has to do with in part has to do with the personality of the decision makers tendency to engage in mixed messaging although that's not just a foable of this current administration this is a problem that senior decision makers have had repeatedly and also a tendency to focus on capabilities at the expense of credibility and understanding how sometimes messaging that is intended for our domestic audience has an impact on foreign actors in ways that undercuts our ability to do deter or compel. Admiral Cooper, the Sentcom commander, was on TV yesterday and he said he's not at all worried about any munition shortages or availability and that they're prepared for any contingency. Mark, you folks especially have done a lot of pathbreaking work on how we've chewed through key munitions throughout the course of this war ever since it started earlier this year. It's hard to believe how long it's been going on actually. Do you think Admiral Cooper is I'm not going to ask you if he's lying. Do you think Admiral Cooper is being accurate here? If you just look at Sentcom, I think that's fair. That is, if the war with Iran were to continue, we have enough munitions to conduct that. We looked at seven munitions that are used heavily against Iran and would be used in the Western Pacific. Overall, we've used about half. So that means we have half left. On the other hand, if you open the aperture and you look at >> Yes. If the world isn't just Sencom. Yeah. >> You look at Paycom, I think it's quite different. And we have particularly a problem with defenses against ballistic missiles. The the Patriots, the THAADS, those are down by 60% and there are no substitutes. So when you run out, you're you're out as the Ukrainians are finding out. >> I was going to say, I think the key thing is it's not just the US military's readiness and need for the munitions, it's allies and partners, too. And I many of the Gulf States have been firing off so many of their interceptors. So the line and the queue that's going to form to get the ones that are coming out of off the manufacturing lines next is going to be huge. But I'm going to say something else controversial. I don't think the defensive interceptors are as important for the Pacific because at least for the Patriots and the Thads because in every war game I've been in, the first thing that the red team hits is the radars. So the stock piles don't really matter. I think the shipbased ones are more survivable and more important. And those have also been significantly depleted. So you know your SM3, SM2, SM6. And we saw a preview of that, didn't Iran very early in the war hit, I think a billion dollar radar system just in the opening days. And imagine a more capable adversary. >> Yeah, I think they hit one in Qatar and then they hit the THAD radar in Jordan at MSAB. >> Yeah, without knowing what Admiral Cooper was thinking, I'll just say that, you know, the president has said, his intention is to low-key this for the foreseeable future. You know, of course, the enemy has a vote, so it's possible that if the Iranians were to escalate, our requirements would go way up. But also keep in mind that they have an issue with the same problem we have. They're probably running low on their missile, maybe not drones, but on their missile um stockpile, and they're probably going to be husbanding their resources. And also, they are limited in terms of what they can do because if they were to ramp up escalation against say critical infrastructure in the Gulf, this is an area they're very vulnerable in. So the statement may have been based on a calculation that the Iranians are going to try to operate in this band lower middle range of kind of in intensity of of their operations and they're constrained in in doing so by their own vulnerabilities. I don't know. But certainly if I was in one of the other combatant commands, I'd be concerned about uh their equities. I've heard some people make the argument that listen, we shouldn't be too bothered by burning through all these munitions and the interceptors especially because if war were to kick off with China, we didn't have enough in the first place. So, we just shouldn't be bothered by it. What do you make of that? Uh, it is true we didn't have enough in the first place. Most people had looked at this wargaming Stacy done a lot of that also. I think it all comes to the same conclusion that is that we didn't have enough munitions even before this war began. Having said that, you know, there is a difference between being able to conduct a conflict for 3 weeks as opposed to 6 weeks and those extra 3 weeks, you know, might buy you enough to favorable settlement or might be enough to make it a protracted conflict where the two of you are running low. >> I would say that equally important is that deterrence is perceptual. So, while operationally it might not matter if we don't have enough Patriot reloads, as many as we'd like in Okinawa or wherever they are in the Pacific, that ultimately it is how your adversary is perceiving you and whether they see weakness or not and think that they can exploit it and that they're willing to run the risks associated with it. And the flip side of that is also what your allies are thinking and whether they feel like you are actually going to defend them and capable of defending them. And I think on the interceptors in particular, this is a really important alliance issue across the board because nobody likes getting shot at. You're seeing, I have to imagine, the Gulf States are right now rethinking their strategies because they've proven to be very exposed and suffered a lot of economic damage that it's going to take a long time to recover from. >> The problem for them is that they have nowhere else to go. So I I think that's their that's their dilemma. If I could just provide a little bit of a different perspective based on my you know study of Middle Eastern military history, you look at back at October 73 war which exposed I mean it was a a surprise attack. Israel lost over 2500 fighters in in about 3 weeks but it exposed major problems in their force structure um in their doctrine. Nobody would wish for us to be in this current situation with Iran. But it exposed some important things, certain shortcomings in our way of war, in our doctrine, approach to war stocks, which we're going to address now, and with elacrity. So maybe there'll be some good that will come out of it. Although I hope we don't have any challenges in the near term. This is going to take a while for us to get out of this hole we've dug ourselves into. >> Yeah, let's poke at that a bit because what some people have argued is, well, we're just going to have to make more, make faster. We of course were already on that path. This is something that Deputy Secretary Fineberg has been extremely focused on ever since he took the job and recent political kurfuffle notwithstanding. It's it's still something that was on their way. Now there's more resources. You can't just expand the production line so easily. And this is Ryan's view. This is also not something you could just sprinkle some Silicon Valley magic on. There are some great new non-traditional missile companies producing stuff. We've had them on Cogs of War before as some of our listeners might know. But the capacity issue and also especially when you're speaking about Pack 3es, you can't just make cheaper versions of them. They do very specific advanced kinds of things operating at the edge of their capabilities and multiple technology areas and the way that they work once they're in the air. This isn't something you can just make in your garage. Mark, what do you make of all this? I think we're moving to a range of capabilities. Not just the high-end, which we've heard a lot about, but high, medium, low-end. On Patriot, they are going to develop a medium capability Patriot, less expensive, less capable, but might be able to handle a variety of threats. When you look at ground attack, of course, you've got the high-end with Tomahawk and Jasm, but there a lot of medium range, short range. You hear a lot out of Silicon Valley, a lot of ideas in that space. So, I think you'll see a spectrum, not just the high-end. >> I agree. And I think we absolutely need a hy low mix, but it's harder on the defensive side because the interceptors, you have to have a sophisticated seeker to hit something incoming. And maybe autonomous weapons that use cameras, whether they're of some sort, whether it's a drone or not, will be able to intercept certain types of threats. But even on the offensive side, I think while I'm very much in favor of having lower cost munitions to supplement our stockpiles, there are real limitations to what they can do and what they can be used for. And they're great for regional states, whether it's Iran or Russia that's trying to project power relatively close to their borders. It's a different problem for the United States. And in particular, if you look at the Pacific, Phil Shares and I have a report that should come out this week that looks at two missions in a war with China and what cheap drones could bring to it. In particular, anti-ship and then attacking coastal air bases. And we find that they could be helpful. But if you assume interception rates along the lines of what the Ukrainians are experiencing with drones that they're sending into Russia, 98% of them are being shot down. You still need a lot of them. And by themselves, the cost of an effective salvo is sometimes more than the cost of expensive missile. The real value might be that they can be produced and you have more of them. They can be produced more rapidly. >> You said earlier, Stacy, that the interceptors are something we should be less concerned about for a war in the Pacific. What are the munitions that you think will be more critical and because the radars will get hit? You mentioned, what are some of the munitions that you think are perhaps a more critical class for such contingencies, especially involving Taiwan? For the US versus Taiwan, what I'd really like to see on the ground side is mobile missile defenses, and we don't have that. And maybe we'll have if picks for at least air defense if the army gets version increment 2 that I think is basically the AMR missile in a box, which would be great. I do think that the shipbased air defenses are very important because they can help extend the regional air umbrella and they can move around and bolster the defenses that might be there on the ground, but their mobility and the additional defenses that they have on makes them more survivable than just at an air base where it's sitting there. So on the offensive side, it is things like Elrazom, JASM, moving to SAW, whatever sort of longer range air-to-air missile, the new one that the Air Force is just beginning to produce. I think the AM260, all of that type of stuff. But those are Elrazm. I think we're talking on the order of like 500 that the whole joint force has bought at this point. >> 500 that'll be gone in a day. Bad news doesn't get better with time. So, it's just it's good that we found out now that some of the flaws in our past approach, you know, have become clear and we're acting on them. I'll just say, and again, I will defer to others who know more about this, but I would for low-end systems, I think this is an area where the civilian sector can make a contribution with off the shelf kind of systems. Um, maybe it's at the lower end of lower end spectrum, but I think that's an area where we could probably wrap up quickly. We saw that in Ukraine, it's happened. So, >> cheap cruise missiles would be a great thing. a cheaper cruise missile, something that is not tomahawk priced that can get you like a thousand miles would be a wonderful addition to have I think to the arsenal and that you know the Air Force is pursuing with FAM and the ETV program and I think there's one other that I'm forgetting right now and like absolutely want to do that on the offensive side especially for fixed targets where it's a little bit easier the requirements aren't such that you're going to have to put in really expensive components beyond that I think you're starting to see the wear on the force and obviously the Navy's has been the most prominent example with a carrier that's been out 200ome days. I forget exactly how many. But if we're really going to maintain this sort of blockade against Iran, that's going to require a huge amount of the surface fleet there patrolling all the time. And that wear and tear is even as difficult, if not harder, than the munitions, the longrange missiles. >> You read my mind. That's exactly where I wanted to go next. And that was the perfect transition. Mark, you you're a Marine. You speak Navy. Stacy just said, "We've had these ships out there a long time. We've moved ships that should be frankly in the Pacific into the Gulf. I think we have 17 destroyers alone to help reinforce this blockade against Iran. What is keeping ships deployed due to the readiness of of course obvious things the availability, but the long-term readiness of the force, keeping these ships out there for so long?" There are two issues. I mean, one is there is a part of the force that's designed to be deployed. The strategic trade-off is that they're now all in the Middle East. they aren't in the Western Pacific. They aren't in the Caribbean. So, you've taken the strategic risk of putting them all in one region. And then there's the the risk of ships that either weren't intended to be deployed, so then now they're doing maybe backtoback deployments, and then you're extending deployments, and that wears on the crews. We saw that with the Abraham Lincoln. On the other hand, we we've done this before in Vietnam. you know, we kept uh naval forces, you know, off the coast for a decade. Uh we did >> we had more of them, but yes, >> we did have more of them. If you if the Navy plans for the rotation, I mean, I think that's that's doable, but there's the strategic tradeoff that you're giving up on other regions. >> Where do you think Iran's capabilities go? They've entered this adaptation and innovation cycle in wartime and this intensity that we've seen with Russia and there's a lot of cooperation going on between Russia, China, Iran. There was just this great Wall Street Journal piece about how Russian engineers are working inside Chinese industry in China to enable this. Iran seems to be heading in that direction. Right now we're in this sort of lowgrade period of the conflict right now where it's there's strikes often. I think there were just a couple last night or the night before, but it's not like a highintensity war right now. Iran does have the options to sort of escalate and may have increasingly sophisticated tools in order to do so. What do you all make of that? Starting with you, Mike. >> I have fruit trees in my front yard and every year we prune them in order to get some of the secondary branches you remove them so that the energy goes to the primary branches and you know produces uh more better fruit. And in a way that's what we did with the Iranian military inadvertently. We kind of got rid of much of their air force and got rid of much of their navy which were probably in a lot of ways kind of less productive, less survivable components of their of their armed forces and left them with what the best protected components and most survivable which were their missiles and drones and which were the most effective as well. So I think they're going to double down on that. But the problem with that approach is that as Eric Olsson once wrote in an article in a few years ago where he said, you know, this creates cra path dependencies and potentially a single point of failure if our air missile defenses get better. So it kind of simplifies the task for us that we just have to focus mainly on this threat. They probably will get better. They'll get maybe their missiles will get counter measures or penetration aids from the Russians or the Chinese and they'll be more challenging to deal with. the drones will maybe get faster. They'll have some of the jet powered kind of shahed 131s and 136s. Hopefully, the Gulf countries and maybe the United States will also benefit from Ukrainian experience in dealing the drones. So, I'm not quite sure how it all kind of works itself out, but for the near term, I think they're just they're going to have to double down on what worked and what they have left in a way simplifies the task for us. I think they're already rebuilding and there's evidence that they're getting Chinese assistance like precursor materials for their ballistic missiles and for the fuel for their ballistic missiles and that the Russians they have seen a Ganu has been found uh fired in the Middle East and that's just going to continue but it's not really just the qualitative improvements that worry me because part of the challenge of this is that you have to face a diverse array of threats. So, you're right. It's simpler and that they don't have an air force or a navy, but they're fielding really different weapons that require different types of defenses at every location essentially. And so, and they're focusing on saturation attacks and that ultimately the cost exchange ratio is in their favor. So if they start improving, you know, the Shahed 136 to bring it up to one of the Guran 2 variants and that is less jammable and just more sophisticated if they can start passing targeting information back like our friend Mike Coffin has talked about, the Russians are doing to follow on missiles and then they have just enough ballistic and cruise missiles to seed them into these larger drone salvos that are really really hard to defend. The Iranians have been very badly hurt. We don't really know how badly in the sense that they've been able to control the release of information. They've been struck with 23,000 attacks and the damage that we can see is very great. So, I'm not convinced that they have a lot of reserve capability. Now, it's I think Stafy's quite correct that they are rebuilding. They're getting help to rebuild, but I don't think they have something that they've been holding back and that they're now going to release. I think that they've done everything that they could and called in all of their allies. On that, I let me just say there was a Wall Street Journal report a few days ago that their rebuilding thus far mainly involves components and the assembly of missiles using components that had been stockpiled before the war, which which sounds right to me because I think a great focus or great attention was put on destroying their missile R&D and production infrastructure. Also, to the degree that in the future they're going to want to move that underground. They could potentially move it to some of the missile cities right now, but then you'd have to use there's less space for missiles in there. Or if they want to dig new facilities, that'll take a while. So, they will go and let me just say with regard to drones, that would be something they could do probably in a matter of months. Missiles might take years, but your your point is well taken. I I agree with you, but it'll take them more time, and they're going to want to do it in a way so they're not as vulnerable next time. My impression, and I'm not sure I'm wrong, so you you two might know better than I do. I don't think they've used many of their anti-ship cruise missiles, have they? That's the one weapon that I feel like I haven't heard as much about, and it might just be a reporting bias that there's information that I want to share. >> I think we're mainly out of the range of most of their systems. So, I think you're right. Most of the what they've used have been drones against, you know, the kind of the maritime shipping in the in the Gulf. I think that when they been taking shots at our naval vessels, I think those have probably been anti-hship missiles >> or ballistic they they do have ballistic missiles that have been developed for that purpose. I think they may have been outside the range of some of the, you know, anti-ship cruise missiles they have, but this has not been an information-rich war in terms of, you know, kind of briefings and reporting on what's going on and who's using what. >> But when they have used missiles against our ships, they've tended to use ballistic missiles and they haven't really. I mean, I think there's a South Korean tanker that got hit with anti-hship cruise missiles early in the war, but it is an interesting omission. I don't know if it's a range issue. I don't know what their range is to be honest. Probably hit a lot of the launchers. Yeah. And and the the problem is I I think a lot of those missiles if you they they've the Iranians in in past years have published videos which shows that a lot of those missiles are kept in underground tunnels kind of missile cities just like their ballistic missiles and the drones. So they may have been outside of our reach, but you know, we probably again rubbled the entrances and stuff, but we may have gotten at some of them. You know, apparently got a lot of the mines. They said they're claiming I think 90 95% of the 8,000 mines that they claimed they had. So it's possible they were in less resilient kind of facilities. I don't know. I don't know. >> I think that highlights a major question which is we really don't have a good sense about what their remaining military capability is. is we know it's enough to scare the shipping companies and the insurance companies and to take shots at both our Gulf allies and our ships, but you know whether they can uh just harass or whether they have really a major capabilities still left, we just don't know. >> I agree. But we're seeing like even their minimal harassment capability, they hit an A10. There were several I forget the exact number of F-15 E that got hit at MSAB again. And that's sort of on the far range of their weapons where I would expect them to be more constrained. So, it's surprising to me that they're still able to put that much pressure. And I think there is a real tension with the US's position right now, since they rely so heavily on groundbased aircraft that even based about as far away as they can be and still be in the Middle East, they're vulnerable. So does that mean they have to push them even farther back to, you know, Romania, Bulgaria, Cyprus, and and try to operate from these ridiculous ranges over to continue to have any effect? or are they just going to leave the region >> or we're going to have to start digging underground tube? >> Uh or we just accept the fact that we're going to lose in the airplane every once in a while. >> Well, bringing this back to China, some have argued that this war that the US launched against Iran has actually been bad for China, it hurts China in some way, whether it's energy exposure, highlighting their maritime vulnerabilities, uh degrading a Chinese partner. I don't personally agree with these arguments in the sense that maybe it hurts China, but I think it's hurt us a lot more. But I'd like to get your opinions. >> I think it's hurt the US much more than China. And right now, China's sort of content to sit back while they don't like the disruption and the spike in price to energy. See what the United States military is doing, how it's performing, and watch it expend, you know, scarce resources that aren't going to be able to be quickly repaired. Also, how it's operating. They're watching. They're drawing forces from the Pacific, not just on the Navy side. I know the Air Force has parts of units, if not whole squadrons, deployed to the Middle East. And General Schneider, Pacific Air Force's commander, recently said that they couldn't conduct exercises on the scale that they had been doing uh this past year in the upcoming one. >> I'll just say that one thing though that came out of this war, which I suspect the Chinese knew, but you when you see it, it has a greater impact. They get I get was it a third of their oil from the Gulf? I guess there I think about half or twothirds of their oil comes from abroad and about half of that's from the Gulf and they see that's vulnerable. The US was able to impose a blockade and because of our positional advantage halfway around the world we have the ability to you know put a squeeze on them. Now they had I guess 6 months or so of oil stockpiled. So that's they they've been preparing for that but this is something which I think has to be kind of a something which a wakeup call for them. >> Yeah. A downside for both Russia and China, not just in Iran, but also Venezuela and Cuba, is that that their demonstrated inability to protect their client states. And although the United States has, you know, had enormous problems in the Middle East, we're still able to pummel their ally, their client, and they really couldn't stop us. I'm not sure they see though that the Iranians I I think would defer to, you know, colleagues who focus on China more than I do >> as a client. Yeah, >> they, you know, they're a useful partner or co maybe co-elligerent even. It's just simply maybe that's a little too strong, but they're we're not fighting them now. But they just are a useful source of leverage of the US. But they I don't think there was any kind of implied commitment to Iran and and you know I think the Iranians were disappointed by the Chinese conduct. But I I think it's they don't expect much from Russia and I think they've learned that they can't expect much from China either. I think and also it makes me think Mark of if that argument is true then someone in Moscow could be sitting well even though Ukraine's gone badly for us at least it showed that the US can't protect one of its clients. Like it's sort of like, okay, maybe, but let's look at the strategic picture and the situation we've caught ourselves in. >> Well, I mean, to flip that around, we were able to protect our >> Not from invasion. >> Not from invasion, but >> Ukraine's under much higher military pressure in some ways than Iran is right now. >> The reason that they have held out is because the United States and NATO, you know, have provided immense amounts of munitions and weapons. I mean something that Russia and China have not done. You know they provided you know some capabilities but nothing on the scale of what we've done for Ukraine and if you are country that's trying to make a decision between the US and China is not going to >> seriously downstream diplomatic and balance of power benefits downstream. >> Yes. questions come up about whether the war has damaged deterrence against China, particularly over Taiwan, and the expenditure of munitions has certainly hurt that because going into the war, most people thought we didn't have enough. Now we have even less. But there are two things that push in the other direction. One is the obvious skill of the US military. We've had a hard time connecting that skill with a successful political outcome, but our ability to beat down the Iranian air defenses and essentially bomb anything we wanted in the country, you know, we were able to do with very, very low casualties. You look at Venezuela, we snatched their head of state and took him back to New York, putting him on trial. And the Chinese are very aware that they have no recent combat experience. since their last war was against Vietnam 1979 they did very badly from their literature you know they are very conscious of that so hard to say how they're weighing it but they must be looking at that the other thing is Iran has been able to exert control over the strait Ukraine has been able to exert control over the Black Sea both of them without the traditional attributes of a navy and the Chinese might be looking at the Taiwan straight and wondering if Taiwan might be able to do something like that also Presidents have repeatedly I think had problems in in the postc cold war era thinking in a kind of rigorous way about deterrence. There was a defense science board study I think in 2007 about deterrence skills and how with the end of the cold war the retirement of a lot of officials who had experienced and this was about nuclear deterrence but I think it also applies to conventional deterrence that a lot of our skills in this area have atrophied and when you look back you know we had with President Obama the red the Syrian chemical weapons red line in 2012 and 2013 which when he failed to stand by them we had the next year Russians going into Crimea and then you had the Chinese starting to build these air strips and these islands in the South China Sea and then you had uh President >> Well, that was already happening. >> That started before, but I think it ramped up after that. I think it's fair to say. And then with President Biden, you know, he kind of used the most economical way of kind of threatening the Iranians, saying don't. And then he kept emphasizing their interest in deescalation. And I'll just say in the Middle East, talking about the escalation is like wearing a kick me sign on your back. And then finally, President Trump had consistently dispute fire, but then stepped back. In the in the end, I think emboldened Iran. So I think, and this is a problem, you know, presidents go don't go to war college, and I don't know how you deal with this this problem, but this is a repeat problem we've had. >> Well, I'll just say one quick thing and then I want to give Stacy the last word because we're just about out of time. I largely reject that interpretation of credibility and deterrence. I don't think countries say, "Well, the US did this here in this corner of the world and therefore they will do XY in this other corner of the world." I I don't think that's how most US adversaries think, which isn't to say they don't take lessons from those things, but I don't think it's why they do things. I think, you know, even the most famous argument is that Putin thought that the US would just roll over on Ukraine because of the Afghan withdrawal. I've seen it reported. I'm not convinced. I think countries make decisions based on their interpretation of the balance of power, especially in the region that they're going to go to war in their understanding of relative value of the object and capabilities and but you know it's different different schools of thought. >> It's a data point. It's a data point. >> I tend to agree with you Ryan and I think that if you look at the balance of power and what has happened to US military strength in the Indoacific as a result of the war in Iran, it has shifted in an unfavorable direction towards China. They've seen, you know, the expenditure of so many munitions. They've seen a lot of deployments of forces. I think from a operational perspective, I would expect that they're feeling somewhat validated with their counter intervention strategy, which really focuses on holding bases and surface forces at risk. No US ship has been hit by a missile, thankfully. But Iran is much less capable than China. And China has thousands of long range missiles and much more sophisticated sensors and a network connecting them all together. So from that perspective, I think it would, you know, hurt deterrence. The one thing that might give them pause because they're always weighing the risks too is seeing that Iran has been pummeled to the ground and they haven't conceded. And that should raise questions about going after Taiwan and a society. how much they're willing to withstand in order to maintain their independence. >> Thank you for listening to this episode of the War on the Rocks podcast. Do not forget to check out our membership program at war ontherocks.com/membership and rate us five stars on whatever app you're listening to the show on. It matters. It makes a difference. Stay safe and stay healthy.
